name: PAM8403DR-H
title: PAM8403: 3 W stereo filterless class-D audio amplifier, SOP-16
summary: A two-channel class-D power amplifier with bridge-tied outputs that drive a speaker with no LC output filter. From a 2.5 V to 5.5 V supply it gives 3.2 W into 4 Ω at 10 % THD+N (5 V), with a fixed 24 dB gain, active-low shutdown and mute inputs, under-voltage lock-out, output short-circuit protection and thermal shutdown. Efficiency reaches about 87 % into 8 Ω. It is marked not recommended for new design, with the PAM8406 named in its place.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: Both channels driven from AC-coupled inputs, each output pair wired straight across a speaker with no filter. Each input goes through a 0.47 µF coupling capacitor and a series resistor Ri; VREF has a 0.1 µF capacitor to analog ground. VDD has 1 µF to analog ground; the PVDD rail has 1 µF at each PVDD pin and a 470 µF bulk capacitor to power ground. SHDN and MUTE come in as control lines. NC is joined to analog ground.

parts.note: left input resistor, value not given
right input resistor, value not given

notes: VDD and PVDD are separate rails; analog ground (GND, NC) and power ground (PGND) are separate nets.

circuits.title: Ferrite bead output filter for EMI
circuits.description: One output pair's network for lowering EMI: each output goes through a ferrite bead, and the speaker side of each bead has a 220 pF capacitor to ground. It acts on EMI from about 1 MHz up. The bead to pick has a high impedance at high frequency and a low one at low frequencies.

circuits.title: Performance test setup
circuits.description: The bench arrangement for the performance figures. An audio generator drives the demo board's input; the load sits across the two outputs, which feed an AUX-0025 low-pass filter and then the analyzer. A bench supply powers the board, and every instrument shares ground.
notes: Class-D measurements with the Audio Precision analyzer need the AUX-0025 low-pass filter in front of it.
For efficiency, two 22 µH inductors go in series with the load resistor to stand in for a small speaker.

equations.name: Differential gain

where.AVD: gain from input to the bridged output, dB
where.RF: feedback resistor of the first stage, 142 kΩ at most
where.RI: input resistance of the first stage, 18 kΩ at least

equations.note: The second stage has a fixed gain of 2, so the limits on RF and RI cap the gain at 24 dB.

where.fC: corner frequency of the input high-pass

operation.text: Each channel has two stages. The first sets the gain by the RF to RI ratio; the second inverts it with a fixed gain of 2. The two outputs of a channel are equal in size and 180° apart, driving the speaker as a bridge.
MUTE low turns the outputs off at once, with no fade; high turns them on. The pin has an internal pull-up and can be left open. Supply current while muted is 3.5 mA typ at 5 V.
SHDN low switches off the bias circuits, cutting supply current to under 1 µA. The pin has an internal pull-up and can be left open.

Two capacitors of different kinds: a low-ESR ceramic of typically 1.0 µF as close to the VDD pin as possible for fast transients and switching noise, and 20 µF (ceramic) or more near the amplifier for lower-frequency noise. Decoupling affects THD+N, PSRR and the low-frequency response.

CI and the input resistance RI make a high-pass filter. Small portable speakers reproduce little below 100 Hz to 150 Hz, so a large CI adds cost and size with no gain in sound. CI charges to about half VDD at turn-on through the feedback path; the smaller it is, the smaller the turn-on pop.

CBYP on VREF matters more than any other capacitor round the part. It sets how fast the amplifier starts up from power-on or shutdown, and it filters supply noise from the internal reference that would otherwise show as worse PSRR and THD+N. For the best THD and noise use a 0.47 µF to 1.0 µF ceramic; a larger value cuts the clicks and pops at power on, power off and shutdown.
The outputs turn off when VDD falls to 2.0 V or below and come back once VDD is 2.2 V or more.
A short from output to output or from an output to ground turns the outputs off at once. They come back once the short is gone.

The outputs turn off when the die passes +140 °C; the trip point has a tolerance of 15 °C from part to part. The fault does not latch: the outputs return when the die has cooled by 30 °C, a hysteresis wide enough to avoid motorboating.

With speaker leads shorter than 20 cm, a simple measure is an extra 1000 µF capacitor at the supply terminal. Most designs need a ferrite bead filter on the outputs, which works on EMI from about 1 MHz up. Without an LC filter, a ferrite chip bead in each speaker lead is advised.

operation.topic: Use with an LC output filter
operation.text: With LC filters on the outputs, the speaker must be connected before power is applied, or the part is easily damaged.
Four fresh dry or alkaline cells give over 6.0 V, above the part's limit, and can damage it. Four NiMH cells or three dry or alkaline cells are the recommended supply.
The gain is high, so a large input signal drives the output into clipping as the volume rises, and that can damage the part.
Without LC filters, THD and efficiency measured into a resistor come out worse than into a speaker.
Top marking is PAM8403 over XATYWWLL: X and LL are internal codes, A the assembly code, T the testing code, Y the year and WW the week.
